results.title: Just infinite groups
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A group $G$ is just infinite if it is infinite and every nontrivial normal subgroup of $G$ has finite index in $G$.

results.title: Residually finite groups
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A group $G$ is residually finite if every element $g \ne 1$ of $G$ lies outside some normal subgroup of finite index in $G$.

results.title: Hereditarily just infinite groups
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A group $G$ is hereditarily just infinite (in the sense of Kourovka 15.18) if it is infinite, residually finite, and every nontrivial normal subgroup of $G$, viewed as a group in its own right, is just infinite.

results.title: Kourovka 15.18(a): hereditarily just infinite torsion groups
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Kourovka 15.18(b): linearity of hereditarily just infinite groups
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The proposition that every finitely generated hereditarily just infinite group $G$ is linear, i.e. that there are a field $K$, a natural number $n$ and an injective group homomorphism $G \to \mathrm{GL}_n(K)$.

results.title: Finitely generated hereditarily just infinite torsion groups exist

results.title: Not every finitely generated hereditarily just infinite group is linear
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Vertices of a spherically homogeneous rooted tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a sequence $m : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ of branching indices, the vertices of the spherically homogeneous rooted tree with branching sequence $m$ are the finite words $x_0 x_1 \cdots x_{\ell-1}$ of natural numbers with $x_i < m(i)$ for every $i < \ell$. The length of a word is its level and its prefixes are its ancestors.

results.title: Rigid vertex stabilizer
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\rho$ be a homomorphism from a group $G$ to the group of permutations of the vertices of the rooted tree with branching sequence $m$, and let $v$ be a vertex. The rigid vertex stabilizer of $v$ is the set of elements $g \in G$ such that $\rho(g)$ fixes every vertex that does not have $v$ as a prefix, that is, the elements whose support (the set of vertices they move) lies in the subtree rooted at $v$.

results.title: Rigid level stabilizer
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\rho$ be a homomorphism from a group $G$ to the group of permutations of the vertices of the rooted tree with branching sequence $m$. For a natural number $n$, the $n$-th rigid level stabilizer is the subgroup of $G$ generated by the union of the rigid vertex stabilizers of all vertices at level $n$, that is, of all words of length $n$.

results.title: Growth rate of a finite generating family
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $P$ be a generating family of a group $G$ indexed by $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$, and let $\beta_P(n)$ be the number of elements of $G$ whose word length with respect to $P$ is at most $n$, that is, which are products of at most $n$ members of $P$ and their inverses. The growth rate of $P$ is the real number $\omega(G, P) = \limsup_{n \to \infty} \beta_P(n)^{1/n}$.

results.title: Just infinite groups
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A group $G$ is just infinite if it is infinite and every nontrivial normal subgroup of $G$ has finite index, that is, all proper quotients of $G$ are finite.

results.title: Groups of intermediate growth
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A group $G$ has intermediate growth if it is finitely generated and, for every natural number $k$ and every generating family $P$ of $G$ indexed by $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$, the growth rate of $P$ is at most $1$ (subexponential growth) and $P$ does not have polynomial growth.

results.title: Lower-triangular Toeplitz matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $R$ be a set with a zero element $0$ and let $a = (a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots)$ be a sequence in $R$. The lower-triangular Toeplitz matrix of $a$ is the matrix with rows and columns indexed by $\mathbb{N}$ whose $(i, j)$ entry is $a_{i-j}$ when $j \le i$ and $0$ when $j > i$. In particular it is constant along each diagonal and vanishes strictly above the main diagonal.

results.title: Entries on and below the diagonal of a lower-triangular Toeplitz matrix
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a set with a zero element and $a = (a_0, a_1, \dots)$ a sequence in $R$. For natural numbers $j \le i$, the $(i, j)$ entry of the lower-triangular Toeplitz matrix of $a$ is $a_{i-j}$.

results.title: Entries above the diagonal of a lower-triangular Toeplitz matrix
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Diagonal entries of a lower-triangular Toeplitz matrix
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a set with a zero element and $a = (a_0, a_1, \dots)$ a sequence in $R$. For every natural number $i$, the $(i, i)$ entry of the lower-triangular Toeplitz matrix of $a$ is $a_0$.

results.title: Toeplitz matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A real $(n+1) \times (n+1)$ matrix $A = (a_{ij})$, with rows and columns indexed by $\{0, \dots, n\}$, is Toeplitz if there is a function $c : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $a_{ij} = c(i - j)$ for all $i, j$. Equivalently, $A$ is constant along each of its diagonals.

results.title: Symmetric Toeplitz matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A real $(n+1) \times (n+1)$ matrix $A = (a_{ij})$, with rows and columns indexed by $\{0, \dots, n\}$, is symmetric Toeplitz if there is a function $c : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $c(-k) = c(k)$ for every integer $k$ and $a_{ij} = c(i - j)$ for all $i, j$.

results.title: Toeplitz matrices from coefficients
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A = (a_{ij})$ be a real $(n+1) \times (n+1)$ matrix with rows and columns indexed by $\{0, \dots, n\}$. If $c : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies $a_{ij} = c(i - j)$ for all $i, j$, then $A$ is a Toeplitz matrix.

results.title: Symmetric Toeplitz matrices from even coefficients
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A = (a_{ij})$ be a real $(n+1) \times (n+1)$ matrix with rows and columns indexed by $\{0, \dots, n\}$. If $c : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies $c(-k) = c(k)$ for every integer $k$ and $a_{ij} = c(i - j)$ for all $i, j$, then $A$ is a symmetric Toeplitz matrix.

results.title: Symmetric Toeplitz matrices are Toeplitz
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every real $(n+1) \times (n+1)$ symmetric Toeplitz matrix is a Toeplitz matrix.

results.title: Symmetric Toeplitz matrices are symmetric
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $A = (a_{ij})$ is a real $(n+1) \times (n+1)$ symmetric Toeplitz matrix, with rows and columns indexed by $\{0, \dots, n\}$, then $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all $i, j$.

results.title: Rearick logarithm
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $f$ be a real-valued arithmetic function with $f(1) > 0$, and let $f^{-1}$ be its Dirichlet inverse. The Rearick logarithm of $f$ is the arithmetic function $L(f)$ with $L(f)(0) = 0$, $L(f)(1) = \log f(1)$, and $L(f)(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} f(d) \, f^{-1}(n/d) \log d$ for $n > 1$.

results.title: The Rearick logarithm as a Dirichlet convolution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ be a real-valued arithmetic function with $f(1) = 1$, and let $f^{-1}$ be its Dirichlet inverse. Then the Rearick logarithm of $f$ is the Dirichlet convolution of the pointwise product $n \mapsto f(n) \log n$ with $f^{-1}$.

results.title: Rearick's characterization of multiplicative functions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ be a real-valued arithmetic function with $f(1) > 0$, and let $L(f)$ be its Rearick logarithm. Then $f$ is multiplicative (that is, $f(1) = 1$ and $f(mn) = f(m) f(n)$ whenever $m$ and $n$ are coprime) if and only if $L(f)(m) = 0$ for every natural number $m$ that is not a prime power, including $m = 0$ and $m = 1$.

results.title: Stirling matrices are mutually inverse and lower triangular
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $N$ be a natural number, and let $A$ and $B$ be the $N \times N$ integer matrices with rows and columns indexed by $0, 1, \dots, N-1$ and entries $A_{ij} = (-1)^{i-j} c(i,j)$ and $B_{ij} = S(i,j)$, where $c(i,j)$ is the unsigned Stirling number of the first kind and $S(i,j)$ the Stirling number of the second kind. results.title: Shifted Stirling matrix of the second kind
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $m$ and $n$, the shifted Stirling matrix $S^{[m]}(n)$ is the $n \times n$ matrix over $\mathbb{Q}$ whose $(i, j)$ entry is the Stirling number of the second kind $S(i + m, j)$, for $1 \le i, j \le n$.

results.title: Shift zero gives the Stirling matrix of the second kind
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, the shifted Stirling matrix $S^{[0]}(n)$, the $n \times n$ rational matrix with entries $S(i + 0, j)$ for $1 \le i, j \le n$, equals the Stirling matrix of the second kind $S(n)$, the $n \times n$ rational matrix with entries $S(i, j)$; here $S(i, j)$ denotes the Stirling numbers of the second kind.

results.title: First column of a shifted Stirling matrix
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $m$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $n > 0$, and let $S^{[m]}(n)$ be the $n \times n$ rational matrix with entries $S(i + m, j)$ for $1 \le i, j \le n$, where $S(i, j)$ denotes the Stirling numbers of the second kind. Every entry of the first column of $S^{[m]}(n)$ equals $1$: $S(i + m, 1) = 1$ for $1 \le i \le n$.

results.title: Stirling matrix of the first kind
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, the Stirling matrix of the first kind $s(n)$ is the $n \times n$ matrix with rational entries $s(n)_{i,j} = s(i, j)$ for $1 \le i, j \le n$, where $s(i, j)$ is the signed Stirling number of the first kind. Its entries above the diagonal are zero, since $s(i, j) = 0$ for $j > i$.

results.title: Diagonal of the Stirling matrix of the first kind
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, every diagonal entry of the Stirling matrix of the first kind $s(n)$ equals $1$, that is, $s(n)_{i,i} = 1$ for $1 \le i \le n$.

results.title: Upper bidiagonal matrix V(n)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, $V(n)$ is the $n \times n$ matrix over $\mathbb{Q}$, with rows and columns indexed by $1, \dots, n$, whose entries are $V_{i,i} = i$ on the diagonal, $V_{i,i+1} = 1$ just above the diagonal, and $0$ elsewhere.

results.title: Diagonal entries of the bidiagonal matrix V(n)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, let $V(n)$ be the $n \times n$ rational upper bidiagonal matrix with $V(n)_{i,i} = i$, $V(n)_{i,i+1} = 1$ and all other entries $0$, indices running over $1, \dots, n$. Then $V(n)_{i,i} = i$ for every $1 \le i \le n$.

results.title: Upper triangular matrix Ṽ(n)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, $\tilde V(n)$ is the $n \times n$ matrix over $\mathbb{Q}$, with rows and columns indexed by $1, \dots, n$, whose $(i, j)$ entry is $(-1)^{j-i} (i-1)!/j!$ if $i \le j$ and $0$ if $i > j$.

results.title: Diagonal entries of the matrix Ṽ(n)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, let $\tilde V(n)$ be the $n \times n$ upper triangular matrix over $\mathbb{Q}$, with rows and columns indexed by $1, \dots, n$, whose $(i, j)$ entry is $(-1)^{j-i} (i-1)!/j!$ if $i \le j$ and $0$ if $i > j$. Then for every $i$ with $1 \le i \le n$, the $(i, i)$ entry of $\tilde V(n)$ is $1/i$.

results.title: Shifted Vandermonde matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, the shifted Vandermonde matrix $E(n)$ is the $n \times n$ matrix with rational entries $E(n)_{i,j} = (j + 1)^{i-1}$ for $1 \le i, j \le n$.

results.title: First row of the shifted Vandermonde matrix
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n \ge 1$, every entry in the first row of the shifted Vandermonde matrix $E(n)$ equals $1$, that is, $E(n)_{1,j} = 1$ for $1 \le j \le n$.

results.title: Signed count of compositions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $N$ and a property $P$ of compositions of $N$, the signed count of the compositions of $N$ satisfying $P$ is the number of them with an odd number of parts minus the number with an even number of parts. Equivalently, it is the sum of $(-1)^{\ell(c) + 1}$ over all compositions $c$ of $N$ satisfying $P$, where $\ell(c)$ is the number of parts of $c$.

results.title: Signed count of the compositions of zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The only composition of $0$ is the empty one, which has no parts and so is even. Hence the signed count of all compositions of $0$, the number of odd compositions minus the number of even ones, is $-1$.

results.title: Huang's placement condition for small parts
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $k$ be a natural number. A finite sequence $(a_0, \dots, a_{\ell - 1})$ of natural numbers satisfies the placement condition for $k$ when every entry $a_i < k$ has a preceding entry and a following entry, the preceding entry satisfies $a_{i-1} \ge k$, and the following entry $a_{i+1}$ is either the last entry (that is, $i + 2 = \ell$) or satisfies $a_{i+1} > k$.

results.title: Sequences without small parts satisfy Huang's placement condition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If every entry of a finite sequence of natural numbers is at least $k$, then the sequence satisfies Huang's placement condition for $k$, vacuously.

results.title: Legendre's identity for partitions into distinct parts
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, let $E(n)$ and $O(n)$ be the numbers of partitions of $n$ into distinct parts with an even and an odd number of parts, respectively. If $2n = j(3j + 1)$ or $2n = j(3j - 1)$ for some integer $j \ge 0$, then $E(n) - O(n) = (-1)^j$; otherwise $E(n) - O(n) = 0$.

results.title: Signed count of compositions with parts greater than one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $n \ge 0$, among the compositions of $n + 1$ whose parts are all greater than $1$, the number with an odd number of parts minus the number with an even number of parts is $(-1)^j$ if $n = 3j + 1$ or $n = 3j + 2$ for some $j \ge 0$, and $0$ otherwise.

results.title: Signed count of compositions with parts at least $k$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $k, n \ge 1$. Among the compositions of $n + k - 1$ whose parts are all at least $k$, the number with an odd number of parts minus the number with an even number of parts equals $\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor (n-1)/k \rfloor} (-1)^j \binom{n-1-j(k-1)}{j}$.

results.title: Nyirenda's identity for distinct parts modulo a multiple of four
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $r \ge 1$ and $n$ be natural numbers, and let $E(n)$ and $O(n)$ be the numbers of partitions of $n$ into distinct parts, each congruent to $0$, $2r + 1$ or $2r - 1$ modulo $4r$, with an even and an odd number of parts, respectively. If $n = j(2rj + 1)$ or $n = j(2rj - 1)$ for some integer $j \ge 0$, then $E(n) - O(n) = (-1)^j$; otherwise $E(n) - O(n) = 0$.

results.title: Nyirenda's identity for distinct parts modulo an odd number

If $2n = j((2r + 1)j + 1)$ or $2n = j((2r + 1)j - 1)$ for some integer $j \ge 0$, then $E(n) - O(n) = (-1)^j$; otherwise $E(n) - O(n) = 0$.

results.title: Bindings stored in a perfect hash table

results.title: Entries of a perfect hash table are its stored bindings
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every two-level perfect hash table, every key $k$ and every value $v$, the pair $(k, v)$ belongs to the list of entries of the table (the contents of its occupied secondary slots, bucket by bucket) if and only if some secondary slot of the table holds the binding $(k, v)$.

results.title: The empty perfect hash table is valid
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every primary hash function, every positive number of buckets, and every choice of secondary table sizes and secondary hash functions, the empty two-level perfect hash table with these parameters is valid: no slot is occupied, so both conditions of validity hold vacuously.

results.title: The empty perfect hash table stores nothing

results.title: Soundness of perfect-hash lookup
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a two-level perfect hash table with decidable equality on keys, and with no validity hypothesis, if looking up a key $k$ returns a value $v$, then some secondary slot of the table holds the binding $(k, v)$.

results.title: Lookup finds every stored binding
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a valid two-level perfect hash table, if the binding $(k, v)$ is held in some slot of the table, then looking up $k$ returns $v$.

results.title: Stored values in a valid perfect hash table are unique
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a valid two-level perfect hash table, if some secondary slots hold bindings $(k, v_1)$ and $(k, v_2)$ with the same key $k$, then $v_1 = v_2$.

results.title: Lookup fails exactly on unstored keys
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a valid two-level perfect hash table and any key $k$, looking up $k$ returns no value if and only if there is no value $v$ such that the binding $(k, v)$ is held in some slot of the table.

results.title: Lookup finds every entry
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a valid two-level perfect hash table, if the pair $(k, v)$ belongs to the list of entries of the table, then looking up $k$ returns $v$.

results.title: Successful perfect-hash lookups return entries
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a two-level perfect hash table with decidable equality on keys, if looking up a key $k$ returns a value $v$, then $(k, v)$ belongs to the list of entries of the table. No validity hypothesis is needed.

results.title: Lookup in the empty perfect hash table fails
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every primary hash function, every number of buckets $b > 0$, all secondary table sizes and secondary hash functions, and every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the empty table returns no value.

results.title: The empty perfect hash table has no entries
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every primary hash function, every number of buckets $b > 0$, and all secondary table sizes and secondary hash functions, the list of entries of the empty table is the empty list.

results.title: Occupancy of a perfect-hashing bucket
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a two-level perfect hash table and a bucket $i$, the occupancy $n_i$ of bucket $i$ is the number of slots of the secondary table of bucket $i$ that hold a binding. It is the $n_i$ of the Fredman–Komlós–Szemerédi analysis.

results.title: Total number of keys of a perfect hash table
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a two-level perfect hash table, write $n_i$ for the number of occupied secondary slots of bucket $i$. The total number of keys of the table is $\sum_i n_i$, the number of occupied secondary slots over all buckets.

results.title: Total secondary space of a perfect hash table
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a two-level perfect hash table, write $m_i$ for the number of slots of the secondary table of bucket $i$. The total secondary space of the table is $\sum_i m_i$, the number of secondary slots over all buckets.

results.title: FKS square sizing rule

results.title: Bucket occupancy is at most the secondary table size

results.title: Each secondary table fits in the total secondary space

results.summary: In a two-level perfect hash table with $b$ buckets and secondary sizes $m_0, \dots, m_{b-1}$, every bucket $i < b$ satisfies $m_i \le \sum_{j < b} m_j$, the total secondary space.

results.title: Total secondary space under square sizing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a two-level perfect hash table satisfying the FKS sizing rule, and write $n_i$ for the number of occupied secondary slots of bucket $i$. Then the total secondary space of $T$ equals $\sum_i n_i^2$, the sum over all buckets $i$.

results.title: Quadratic space bound under square sizing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a two-level perfect hash table satisfies the FKS sizing rule, then its total secondary space is at most the square of its total number of keys.

results.title: Backward generator of the Wright–Fisher diffusion with selection
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The backward generator of the Wright–Fisher diffusion with genic selection, time in units of `2N` generations and scaled selection coefficient `σ = 2Ns`: `(L_σ u)(x) = x (1 - x) / 2 · u''(x) + σ x (1 - x) · u'(x)`.

results.title: Kimura's fixation probability
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Kimura's fixation probability of an allele at initial frequency `x` with scaled selection coefficient `σ = 2Ns`: `(1 - e^{-2σx}) / (1 - e^{-2σ})`, and `x` in the neutral case.

results.title: Kimura–Ohta mean absorption time of a neutral allele
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Kimura–Ohta mean time to absorption (loss or fixation) of a neutral allele at frequency `x`, in units of `2N` generations: `-2 (x log x + (1 - x) log (1 - x))`. In generations this is `-4N (x ln x + (1 - x) ln (1 - x))`.

results.title: Wright's stationary density of the Wright–Fisher diffusion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Wright's (unnormalized) stationary density of the Wright–Fisher diffusion with scaled mutation rates `α` (towards the allele) and `β` (away from it): `x ^ (2α - 1) (1 - x) ^ (2β - 1)` (real powers).

results.title: Slope constant of Kimura's fixation probability
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The constant `K σ` such that `(kimuraFixation σ)' x = K σ · e^{-2σx}`: `1` if `σ = 0`, and `2σ / (1 - e^{-2σ})` otherwise.

results.title: Denominator of Kimura's formula is nonzero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `σ ≠ 0` the denominator `1 - e^{-2σ}` of Kimura's formula does not vanish.

results.title: Kimura's fixation probability vanishes at frequency zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: An allele that is absent is never fixed.

results.title: Kimura's fixation probability equals one at frequency one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: An allele that is already fixed stays fixed.

results.title: Neutral fixation probability equals the initial frequency
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Neutral case: the fixation probability equals the initial frequency.

results.title: Slope constant of Kimura's formula is nonzero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The slope constant of Kimura's formula never vanishes.

results.title: Derivative of Kimura's fixation probability at a point
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The derivative of Kimura's fixation probability: `u'(x) = K σ · e^{-2σx}`.

results.title: Continuity of Kimura's fixation probability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Kimura's fixation probability is continuous in the initial frequency.

results.title: Derivative of Kimura's fixation probability as a function
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The derivative of Kimura's fixation probability, as a function.

results.title: Kimura (1962)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The fixation probability solves the backward equation `x (1 - x) / 2 · u'' + σ x (1 - x) · u' = 0` (everywhere).

results.title: Uniqueness of the fixation probability (Kimura 1962)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If `u` is continuous on `[0, 1]`, differentiable on `(0, 1)` with derivative `u'` differentiable on `(0, 1)`, solves the backward equation `L_σ u = 0` on `(0, 1)`, and satisfies `u 0 = 0`, `u 1 = 1`, then `u` is Kimura's fixation probability on `[0, 1]`.

results.title: Uniqueness of the fixation probability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Uniqueness of the fixation probability, `C²` form: a function continuous on `[0, 1]`, `C²` on `(0, 1)`, solving `L_σ u = 0` on `(0, 1)` with `u 0 = 0`, `u 1 = 1` equals Kimura's fixation probability on `[0, 1]`.

results.title: Nonnegativity of Kimura's fixation probability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Kimura's fixation probability is nonnegative at nonnegative frequencies, for every selection coefficient `σ`.

results.title: Kimura's fixation probability is at most one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Kimura's fixation probability is at most `1` at frequencies `y ≤ 1`, for every selection coefficient `σ`.

results.title: Kimura's fixation probability lies in the unit interval
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Kimura's fixation probability is a probability on `[0, 1]`.

results.title: Advantageous alleles fix more often than their initial frequency
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Advantageous alleles (`σ > 0`) are fixed with probability strictly larger than their initial frequency `x ∈ (0, 1)`.

results.title: Neutral mean absorption time vanishes at frequency zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The neutral mean absorption time vanishes at `x = 0`.

results.title: Neutral mean absorption time vanishes at frequency one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The neutral mean absorption time vanishes at `x = 1`.

results.title: Derivative of the neutral mean absorption time
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Kimura–Ohta (1969)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The neutral mean absorption time solves `L_0 T = -1` on `(0, 1)`.

results.title: Decay of heterozygosity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `H(x) = 2x(1 - x)` is an eigenfunction of the neutral generator with eigenvalue `-1`, so `E[H_t] = H_0 e^{-t}` (time in units of `2N` generations).

results.title: Moment duality with Kingman's coalescent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Moment duality with Kingman's coalescent at generator level: the neutral generator maps `y ↦ y ^ n` to `C(n, 2) (x ^ (n - 1) - x ^ n)`, which is the generator of the block-counting process (jumps `n → n - 1` at rate `C(n, 2)`) applied to `n ↦ x ^ n`.

results.title: Wright's stationary density (zero-flux form)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: On `(0, 1)`, with infinitesimal variance `a(x) = x (1 - x)` and mutation drift `b(x) = α (1 - x) - β x`, Wright's density `π(x) = x ^ (2α - 1) (1 - x) ^ (2β - 1)` satisfies `(a π)' = 2 b π`, i.e. the stationary forward (Fokker–Planck) equation `½ (a π)' - b π = 0` with zero probability flux.

results.title: Normalization of Wright's density
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `α, β > 0` the stationary density integrates to the Beta function `B(2α, 2β) = Γ(2α) Γ(2β) / Γ(2α + 2β)`, so `wrightDensity α β x / B(2α, 2β)` is the Beta`(2α, 2β)` probability density on `(0, 1)`.

results.title: Wright's density has finite positive total mass
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `α, β > 0` Wright's density has a finite, positive total mass on `(0, 1)`.

results.title: Integrability of Wright's density on the unit interval
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `α, β > 0` Wright's density is integrable on `[0, 1]`.

results.title: Heterozygosity decay in one Wright–Fisher generation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the number `X` of copies of an allele among `M` gene copies (`M = 2N` for diploids) is `Binomial(M, x)`, then the new frequency `p' = X / M` satisfies `E[2 p' (1 - p')] = (1 - 1/M) · 2x(1 - x)`.

results.title: Wright–Fisher generator with two-way mutation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The backward generator of the Wright–Fisher diffusion with two-way mutation, time in units of `2N` generations and scaled mutation rates `θ₁ = 4N u₁` (towards the allele) and `θ₂ = 4N u₂` (away from it): `(L f)(x) = x (1 - x) / 2 · f''(x) + (θ₁ (1 - x) - θ₂ x) / 2 · f'(x)`.

results.title: Mutation generator without mutation is the neutral generator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Without mutation the generator is the neutral Wright–Fisher generator `generator 0`.

results.title: Beta density as Wright's stationary density
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: On `(0, 1)` the Beta`(θ₁, θ₂)` density is Wright's unnormalized density in the scaled rates `α = θ₁ / 2`, `β = θ₂ / 2`, divided by the Beta function `B(θ₁, θ₂)`.

results.title: Smoothness of the Beta density on the open unit interval
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Beta`(θ₁, θ₂)` density is analytic (`C^ω`), in particular smooth, on `(0, 1)`, so the derivatives in `flux_betaPDFReal` and `forwardEquation_betaPDFReal` exist.

results.title: Zero probability flux (Wright 1931)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: On `(0, 1)` the Beta`(θ₁, θ₂)` density `π` satisfies `½ (x (1 - x) π)' - (θ₁ (1 - x) - θ₂ x) / 2 · π = 0`. The identity holds for all real `θ₁, θ₂` (it is linear in `π`; Mathlib's density is identically `0` when `B(θ₁, θ₂) = 0`); `π` is a probability density when `θ₁, θ₂ > 0` (`isProbabilityMeasureBeta`).

results.title: Stationary forward equation (Wright 1931)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: On `(0, 1)` the Beta`(θ₁, θ₂)` density `π` solves the stationary Fokker–Planck equation `½ (a π)'' - (b π)' = 0` with `a(x) = x (1 - x)` and `b(x) = (θ₁ (1 - x) - θ₂ x) / 2`. Holds for all real `θ₁, θ₂` (see `flux_betaPDFReal`).

results.title: Integrability of the mutation generator against the Beta density
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `θ₁, θ₂ > 0` and `f` twice continuously differentiable on `[0, 1]`, `L f · π` is integrable on `[0, 1]`, so the integral in `integral_mutationGenerator_mul_betaPDFReal` is a genuine (not junk) value.

results.title: Weak stationarity of Wright's law (density form)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `θ₁, θ₂ > 0` and every `f` twice continuously differentiable on `[0, 1]`, `∫₀¹ (L f)(x) π(x) dx = 0` for the Beta`(θ₁, θ₂)` density `π`. (`L f` uses `deriv`, which agrees with the one-sided derivatives inside `(0, 1)`; its values at the endpoints do not affect the integral.) The proof is integration by parts: `L f · π = (x ^ θ₁ (1 - x) ^ θ₂ f' / (2 B(θ₁, θ₂)))'` on `(0, 1)` because the flux vanishes, and this…

results.title: Integrability of the mutation generator under Wright's stationary law
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `θ₁, θ₂ > 0` and `f` twice continuously differentiable on `[0, 1]`, `L f` is integrable against Wright's stationary law `Beta(θ₁, θ₂)`.

results.title: Weak stationarity of Wright's law (Wright 1931; Ewens 2004, ch. 4)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `θ₁, θ₂ > 0` and every `f` twice continuously differentiable on `[0, 1]`, `∫ L f d(Beta(θ₁, θ₂)) = 0`.

results.title: Mutation generator applied to the allele frequency
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The generator applied to the frequency itself is the mutation drift: `L x = (θ₁ (1 - x) - θ₂ x) / 2`.

results.title: Mutation generator applied to heterozygosity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The generator applied to the heterozygosity `H(x) = 2x (1 - x)`: `L H = -2x (1 - x) + (θ₁ (1 - x) - θ₂ x) (1 - 2x)` (drift decreases `H` at rate `1`, mutation restores it).

results.title: Allele frequency after one generation of two-way mutation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Allele frequency after one generation of two-way mutation, before random sampling: an `a` copy mutates to `A` with probability `u₁` and an `A` copy to `a` with probability `u₂`, so the frequency `x` of `A` becomes `(1 - u₂) x + u₁ (1 - x) ∈ [0, 1]`.

results.title: Drift of the Wright–Fisher chain with mutation (Ewens 2004, ch. 4)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: One generation of the Wright–Fisher chain on `M` gene copies (`M = 2N`): mutation moves the frequency `x` to `p' = mutatedFreq u₁ u₂ x`, then the new count is `Binomial(M, p')`. With `u₁ = θ₁ / (2M)`, `u₂ = θ₂ / (2M)` (`θᵢ = 4N uᵢ`), the expected change of frequency per `2N = M` generations is exactly the drift coefficient of `mutationGenerator`: `M · (E[k / M] - x) = (θ₁ (1 - x) - θ₂ x) / 2`, for every `M`.

results.title: Infinitesimal variance of the Wright–Fisher chain with mutation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In the setting of `integral_binomial_mutatedFreq_drift`, the scaled second moment of the frequency change is `M · E[(k / M - x) ^ 2] = p' (1 - p') + (θ₁ (1 - x) - θ₂ x) ^ 2 / (4M)` with `p' = mutatedFreq u₁ u₂ x = x + (θ₁ (1 - x) - θ₂ x) / (2M)`. As `M → ∞` with `θ₁, θ₂, x` fixed this tends to `x (1 - x)`, the diffusion coefficient of `mutationGenerator` (the limit itself is not stated here).

results.title: Daetwyler–Dudbridge formula
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With sampling variance `s² = 1 / N`, `r²_g = N h² / (N h² + M)`.

results.title: Training genotype matrix with orthogonal standardized columns
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The training genotype matrix has orthogonal columns with sum of squares `N`, `∑ i, X i k * X i l = N [k = l]`; for centered columns this says that the markers are uncorrelated, with unit sample variance, in the training sample.

results.title: Effect-estimate model derived from the LD-score model
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The effect-estimate model obtained from the LD-score model when the effects are estimated by the normalized scores `β̂ = Xᵀ y / N` on a training matrix with orthogonal standardized columns: the error is `e k = ∑ i, X i k ε i / N` and its sampling variance is `(1 - h²) / N`.

results.title: Estimates of the derived model are normalized scores
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The estimates of `ofLDScore` are the normalized scores `Xᵀ y / N` of the LD-score model.

results.title: Polygenic-score accuracy in the LD-score model
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With orthogonal standardized training columns, `β̂ = Xᵀ y / N` and residual variance `1 - h²`, `r²_g = N h² / (N h² + M (1 - h²))`. The cited `N h² / (N h² + M)` takes the residual variance to be `1`.

results.title: Marginal least-squares estimate of a marker effect
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The marginal least-squares estimate `x_jᵀ y / x_jᵀ x_j` of marker `j` (single-marker regression without intercept, on centered genotypes and phenotype as in Yang et al. 2012).

results.title: Diagonal of the genotype Gram matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The diagonal `D = diag(XᵀX)` of the Gram matrix.

results.title: Genotype-phenotype cross products from marginal estimates
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `Xᵀ y = D β̂` for the marginal estimates `β̂` (Yang et al. 2012). This holds for every genotype matrix: a column with `x_jᵀ x_j = 0` is zero, so both sides vanish there.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: COJO joint estimate (Yang et al. 2012, eq. (5)): the joint least-squares estimate `(XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀ y` equals `(XᵀX)⁻¹ D β̂` in terms of the marginal estimates `β̂`, so it can be computed from summary statistics and `XᵀX`. (Stated for every `X`; it is the least-squares estimate when `XᵀX` is invertible.)

results.title: Joint estimate equals marginal estimates for uncorrelated markers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For markers uncorrelated in the sample (`XᵀX` diagonal) without zero columns, the joint estimate is the vector of marginal estimates.

results.title: Conditional estimate of second-block effects (COJO)
results.caption: Definition

results.title: COJO conditional algebraic formula from summary statistics

results.title: Conditional estimate as a fit to the first-block residual
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Unconditionally, the conditional formula equals the nonsingular-inverse formula applied to the algebraic residual `y - X₁ ((X₁ᵀX₁)⁻¹ X₁ᵀ y)`. If both Gram determinants are units, these are the successive least-squares fits on blocks 1 and 2. With a singular Gram matrix they need not minimize residual error. results.title: Stratified LD score
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The stratified normalized-cross-product score `ℓ(j, C) = ∑_{k ∈ C} (X_jᵀ X_k / N)²`. For a standardized genotype matrix this is the stratified LD score of marker `j` with respect to annotation category `C` (Finucane et al. 2015).

results.title: Stratified LD-score model
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: The stratified LD-score model (Finucane et al. 2015), at the level of raw second moments: annotation categories `cat c ⊆ {markers}` (possibly overlapping), per-category contributions `tau c`, effects with `∫ β k β l = [k = l] ∑_c τ_c [k ∈ cat c]`, noise with `∫ ε i ε i' = σ²_e [i = i']`, effects orthogonal to noise. The cited model normalizes the phenotypic variance so that `σ²_e ≈ 1`; the confounding term `N a` is…

results.title: Phenotype in the stratified LD-score model
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The phenotype `y = X β + ε`.

results.title: Normalized score in the stratified LD-score model
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The `N`-normalized score `β̂ j = X_jᵀ y / N`.

results.title: Association statistic in the stratified LD-score model
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The association statistic `χ² j = N β̂ j ²`.

results.title: Expected association statistic in the stratified LD-score model
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The exact expectation of the association statistic in the stratified model, for any genotype matrix: `𝔼[χ² j] = N ∑_c τ_c ℓ(j, cat c) + σ²_e (∑ i, X i j ²) / N`.

results.title: Stratified LD-score regression
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Stratified LD-score regression (Finucane et al. 2015): for a standardized genotype matrix and `N ≠ 0`, `𝔼[χ² j] = N ∑_c τ_c ℓ(j, cat c) + σ²_e`. Full-matrix standardization makes every normalized cross product in `stratLDScore` a sample correlation.

results.title: One causal variant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: One causal variant (the LD-proxy noncentrality; Pritchard & Przeworski 2001): if the genotype matrix is standardized and the only category is the single causal marker `c` with variance `τ`, then for a marker `m` and `N ≠ 0`, `𝔼[χ² m] = N τ r m c ² + σ²_e`.

results.title: In-sample LD correlation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The in-sample normalized cross product `∑_{i ∈ S} X i j X i k / |S|` of markers `j`, `k` in the sample `S` of a pool of individuals (the sample LD correlation for a matrix standardized within `S`).

results.title: Bivariate LD-score model
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: The bivariate LD-score model (Bulik-Sullivan et al. 2015b), at the level of the cross second moments that enter `𝔼[z₁ z₂]`: a pool of `n` genotyped individuals with genotype matrix `X`, two GWAS samples `S₁`, `S₂` of the pool (possibly overlapping), effects `β₁`, `β₂` with `∫ β₁ k β₂ l = (ρ_g / M) [k = l]` (genetic covariance `ρ_g`), noises `ε₁`, `ε₂` with `∫ ε₁ i ε₂ i' = ρ_e [i = i']` (residual cross-moment `ρ_e`…

results.title: Scaled marginal score for the first trait
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The scaled marginal score `z₁ j = √N₁ X_jᵀ y₁ / N₁` of marker `j` for trait 1, computed on `S₁` with `y₁ = X β₁ + ε₁`. The model does not assert the normalization needed for a z-score.

results.title: Scaled marginal score for the second trait
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The analogous scaled marginal score `z₂ j` of marker `j` for trait 2, computed on `S₂`.

results.title: Cross-trait scaled-score identity, exact form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With `N₁ = |S₁|`, `N₂ = |S₂|`, `𝔼[z₁ j z₂ j] = √(N₁ N₂) (ρ_g / M) ∑_k r¹ j k r² j k + ρ_e (∑_{i ∈ S₁ ∩ S₂} X i j ²) / √(N₁ N₂)`, with the in-sample normalized cross products `r¹`, `r²` (`sampleCorr`).

results.title: Equal normalized-cross-product specialization of the residual cross-moment identity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the two samples have the same normalized cross products with marker `j` and the overlap marker is standardized at `j` (`∑_{i ∈ S₁ ∩ S₂} X i j ² = N_s`), then `𝔼[z₁ j z₂ j] = √(N₁ N₂) ρ_g ℓ_j / M + ρ_e N_s / √(N₁ N₂)`. Here `ρ_e` is only the residual cross-moment specified by `CrossTraitModel`; this theorem does not state the Bulik-Sullivan phenotypic-correlation overlap formula or establish z-score normalization.

results.title: Number of individuals in a case-control genotype table
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The number of individuals `N = ∑ (r i + s i)`.

results.title: Numerator of the Cochran–Armitage trend statistic
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The trend numerator `U = ∑ i, i (r i S - s i R)` with `R = ∑ r`, `S = ∑ s`.

results.title: Pooled genotype-score variance
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The pooled genotype-score variance `∑ i² n_i / N - (∑ i n_i / N)²`, `n_i = r i + s i`.

results.title: Cochran–Armitage trend statistic
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Cochran–Armitage trend statistic with scores `0, 1, 2` (Armitage 1955): `N U² / (R S (N ∑ i² n_i - (∑ i n_i)²))`.

results.title: Squared correlation of case status and genotype score
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The squared sample correlation of case status (`1` for cases, `0` for controls) and the genotype score over the `N` individuals of the table.

results.title: Pooled allele frequency
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The pooled frequency `p = ∑ i n_i / (2 N)` of the counted allele.

results.title: Pearson's chi-squared statistic of a 2 × 2 table
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Pearson's statistic `n (a d - b c)² / ((a + b)(c + d)(a + c)(b + d))` of a `2 × 2` table `[[a, b], [c, d]]` with `n = a + b + c + d`.

results.title: Allelic test statistic
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The allelic test: Pearson's statistic of the `2 × 2` table of case and control allele counts (`2N` alleles).

results.title: The trend test is `N r²`
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The trend test is `N r²` (Armitage 1955): the Cochran–Armitage statistic is `N` times the squared sample correlation of case status and genotype score. (In degenerate tables, where a denominator vanishes, both sides are `0` by the convention `x / 0 = 0`.)

results.title: Departure of the genotype-score variance from Hardy–Weinberg
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The observed score variance minus the Hardy–Weinberg score variance `2 p q`: `Var - 2 p (1 - p) = (4 n₀ n₂ - n₁²) / (2 N²)`.

results.title: Allelic versus trend test
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Allelic versus trend test (Sasieni 1997): with cases and controls present, a pooled allele frequency strictly between `0` and `1` and a positive score variance, `allelic · 2 p q = trend · Var`.

results.title: The allelic test equals the trend test iff the pooled sample is in Hardy–Weinberg proportions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The allelic test equals the trend test iff the pooled sample is in Hardy–Weinberg proportions (`n₁² = 4 n₀ n₂`; Sasieni 1997), whenever the trend numerator is nonzero.

results.title: Stein's lemma
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Stein's lemma for the normal law `N(μ, v)`, `v > 0`: if `g` is differentiable with derivative `g'` and `g`, `(z - μ) g z` and `g'` are integrable, then `𝔼[(z - μ) g z] = v 𝔼[g' z]` (Stein 1981, Lemma 1).

results.title: Mean fitness of a normally distributed trait
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The mean fitness `w̄(μ) = 𝔼[W z]` of a population whose trait is distributed as `N(μ, v)`.

results.title: Directional selection differential
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The directional selection differential `S = 𝔼[(z - μ) W z] / w̄`: the mean trait of the selected parents, weighting each individual by its fitness, minus the mean trait `μ` before selection. If `w̄ = 0` the division returns the junk value `0`.

results.title: Derivative of mean fitness with respect to the trait mean
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The derivative of mean fitness with respect to the trait mean is `d/dμ w̄(μ) = 𝔼[(z - μ) W z] / v`, for bounded measurable fitness and `v > 0`.

results.title: Lande's equation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Lande's equation for one normally distributed trait (Lande 1979): the selection differential is the phenotypic variance times the derivative of log mean fitness with respect to the trait mean, `S = v · d/dμ log w̄(μ)`.

results.title: The Lande–Arnold selection gradient
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Lande–Arnold selection gradient for one normally distributed trait: for a differentiable bounded fitness function with integrable derivative, `β = S / v = 𝔼[W' z] / w̄`, the average slope of relative fitness `W / w̄` (Lande–Arnold 1983).

results.title: Mean fitness of a multivariate normal trait
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The mean fitness `w̄(μ) = 𝔼[W z]` of a population whose trait vector is distributed as `N(μ, P)`.

results.title: Multivariate directional selection differential
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The directional selection differential `S = 𝔼[W z · (z - μ)] / w̄` of a trait vector distributed as `N(μ, P)`: the fitness-weighted mean trait vector of the selected parents minus the mean `μ` before selection. If `w̄ = 0` it is the junk value `0`.

results.title: Lande's gradient of mean fitness for multivariate traits
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The gradient of mean fitness with respect to the vector of trait means is `∇_μ w̄(μ) = P⁻¹ 𝔼[W z · (z - μ)]`, for positive definite `P` and bounded measurable `W`.

results.title: Lande's equation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Lande's equation (Lande 1979): for a multivariate normal trait vector, the selection differential is the phenotypic covariance matrix applied to the gradient of log mean fitness with respect to the trait means, `S = P ∇_μ log w̄(μ)`.
